description: Hi, I’m Aimee, an Industrial IT student at INES-Ruhengeri (Musanze, Rwanda) into IoT, embedded systems and AI/ML. We’re building Ubuhinzi Sentinel: simple farm advice for Rwandan farmers from NASA data (POWER, FIRMS, GIBS, HLS), in Kinyarwanda, English and French. The app is live; field boundary drawing is still in progress. Looking for: remote sensing/GIS, ML, frontend/UX, someone with farming knowledge, and a pitch person. Join us to build something farmers can really use!
summary:
Ubuhinzi Sentinel (“Agriculture Sentinel”) is a web app that turns free NASA satellite data into simple farming advice in Kinyarwanda.

The problem: NASA data about rain, soil and temperature is free, but it is technical and hard for a smallholder farmer to use. Farmers still plant and protect their crops with little weather information in their own language.

What we built: A farmer opens the app, draws their field on a map and chooses Kinyarwanda, English or French. Every day the app collects NASA rain, soil moisture and temperature data for that location and checks it for drought and flood risk. The farmer sees a traffic light, 🟢 Good, 🟡 Watch or 🔴 Alert, with one clear action for the day. The app shows its data source and confidence, and it is advice only, so farmers are pointed to Meteo Rwanda and MINEMA for official warnings.

Where we are: The app is live and working. NASA POWER data is coarse today, so advice is regional. Next, we will add finer 30 m crop-greenness data (NASA HLS) for field-level advice.

Why it matters: One missed rain can cost a family a season of food. Simple advice in their own language helps farmers act earlier.
details:
What it does and how it works
Ubuhinzi Sentinel turns free NASA satellite data into a simple traffic light (🟢 Good / 🟡 Watch / 🔴 Alert) in Kinyarwanda for Rwandan smallholder farmers. A farmer draws their field on a map or picks a district (Kigali, Bugesera, Musanze, Nyagatare). A daily job pulls NASA POWER rain, temperature and soil moisture, and an explainable rule-based model scores drought and flood risk. The farmer sees one clear message and what to do today, in Kinyarwanda, English or French. Live now: field drawing, POWER-based drought and flood scoring, a 30-day chart, NASA GIBS map layers and the trilingual interface. Still in progress: real HLS 30 m crop greenness (NDVI is currently a labelled proxy).

Benefits
Farmers get advice in their own language, with no charts needed. Every card shows its source, resolution and confidence, and says “no data” instead of showing a made-up number. It is advice only, and it points farmers to Meteo Rwanda and MINEMA for official warnings. It costs the farmer nothing and works on a basic Android phone.

Intended impact
We want to help smallholders act earlier on drought and heavy rain. If the advice saves 10% of a maize yield, that is about 280 kg per hectare, roughly $90 of food or income. Next steps are real field-level greenness from HLS, then SMS/USSD access for basic phones.

Tools
TypeScript, React, Next.js 15, Tailwind CSS, SQL. Recharts and Leaflet for charts and maps. Supabase with PostGIS for storage, and Vercel for hosting and daily jobs. NASA data: POWER, GIBS, EONET, FIRMS, HLS. Other data: OpenStreetMap and CHIRPS for validation. No custom hardware.

Creativity
It is a translator, not a dashboard: the traffic light comes first and the chart second. The whole app switches language instead of mixing lines. Our “55 km to field” story shows why finer satellite data matters. A tester farmer found a soil-moisture error, and we turned it into a validation page comparing POWER with CHIRPS.

Factors we considered
Trust: we show confidence and missing data. Equity: Kinyarwanda first and no cost to farmers. Validity: POWER is a model, not a ground probe, and we state its limits. Local relevance: four regions with different risks, and Rwanda’s growing seasons. Scale: hosting and data costs stay low as users grow.
